l: RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
s: This ACL 2024 Findings paper, “RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering,” is by Zihan Zhang, Meng Fang, and Ling Chen. It studies adaptive retrieval-augmented generation (ARAG): having a large language model decide whether a question needs external retrieval, rather than retrieving for every query. The authors argue that indiscriminate retrieval can hurt performance and raise inference costs. The paper introduces RetrievalQA, a benchmark for this decision problem. Its 1,271 retained short-form questions target new world and long-tail knowledge that models cannot reliably answer from their parameters and therefore require external information. Questions are drawn from RealTimeQA, FreshQA, PopQA, TriviaQA, and ToolQA, then filtered using GPT-4 closed-book answers; 1,514 questions answerable from GPT-2 parametric knowledge are also added to avoid favoring systems that retrieve too often. Sanity checks indicate that the retrieval-required questions are very difficult for models without external knowledge. Experiments compare standard RAG, calibration-based approaches, model-based approaches, Self-RAG, vanilla prompting, and the authors’ method, using retrieval and match accuracy. Retrieval generally improves QA, but Self-RAG is highly dependent on threshold tuning, and vanilla prompting does not consistently improve retrieval decisions as model size grows. Models more readily recognize retrieval needs for new world knowledge than for long-tail knowledge. To address these issues, the authors propose Time-Aware Adaptive REtrieval (TA-ARE), a calibration-free, training-free prompting method. TA-ARE supplies current-date instructions and in-context demonstrations to help models judge whether retrieval is needed. It improves retrieval accuracy by an average of 14.9% and QA accuracy by 6.7% across baselines. Ablations show that time awareness and relevant examples matter, with four demonstrations, two “Yes” and two “No”, performing best. The paper notes limits in dataset sourcing and GPT-4 filtering, its focus on short-form rather than long-form generation, possible noisy or inadequate retrieved documents, and the absence of prompt tuning. The dataset uses public sources, excludes personally identifiable information, and is accompanied by online code and data. The work was supported by the Australian Research Council.

l: adaptive retrieval-augmented generation, RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Adaptive retrieval-augmented generation is a retrieval-augmented generation approach and framework for open-domain QA tasks that retrieves only when necessary, dynamically determining retrieval necessity for queries rather than retrieving indiscriminately. Its central goal is to improve efficiency and the relevance of sourced information. It includes calibration-based and model-based methods, but its effectiveness has been understudied because suitable benchmarks and evaluations were lacking. The work formalizes and evaluates existing approaches, compares TA-ARE results, finds vanilla prompting unreliable for retrieval decisions, and proposes TA-ARE to improve this capability without calibration or additional training.

l: RetrievalQA, RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
s: RetrievalQA is a dataset and benchmark for short-form open-domain question answering, created to assess adaptive retrieval-augmented generation and LLMs’ ability to decide when to retrieve external resources. It comprises 1,271 questions after filtering, spanning diverse topics in new-world and long-tail knowledge. The knowledge needed for these questions is absent from evaluated LLMs, so the set is extremely hard without external knowledge and makes retrieval necessary. It serves as a testbed for existing ARAG methods, including calibration-based and model-based approaches, evaluating retrieval decisions through retrieval accuracy and answer-match accuracy. To avoid bias toward methods that retrieve more often, its construction also included 1,514 discard-set questions answerable using GPT-2’s parametric knowledge. The dataset was curated from publicly available sources, examined for privacy concerns and violations, and is available at https://github.com/hyintell/RetrievalQA.

l: large language models, RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Large language models are technology with distinct sizes and levels of pre-trained knowledge. Through large-scale pre-training, they encode extensive knowledge and can answer straightforward queries without retrieval, but they are static after training, can become outdated, and are weak on long-tail questions. When needed knowledge is absent, they should recognize the gap, say “I don’t know,” and request external retrieval. In retrieval-augmented generation, they answer using instructions, questions, and retrieved relevant documents, or skip retrieval when it is unnecessary. The records study their ability to judge this need: they perceive some knowledge boundaries, especially for new-world knowledge, but Vanilla prompting makes retrieval decisions unreliable. RetrievalQA is designed around missing knowledge, while TA-ARE helps assess retrieval necessity without calibration or additional training; noisy retrieved context can still interfere.

l: existing ARAG methods, RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Existing ARAG methods, evaluated using RetrievalQA, reveal understudied effectiveness, threshold-tuning limitations, and unreliable retrieval decisions.

l: calibration-based methods, RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Calibration-based methods are adaptive retrieval-augmented generation methods that use a predefined hyperparameter to trigger retrieval only when a metric exceeds a threshold. They are effective but suboptimal because thresholds require tuning across datasets and models. The process begins with threshold selection, then metric comparison, retrieval when surpassed, and trade-off balancing between task performance and retrieval efficiency.

l: Vanilla prompting, RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Vanilla prompting is a method that asks a large language model a yes/no question about whether retrieval is needed, then performs retrieval only after Yes. It is inadequate and insufficient for reliable retrieval decisions: retrieval accuracy varies across models and does not scale consistently with model size.

l: Time-Aware Adaptive REtrieval, RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Time-Aware Adaptive REtrieval (TA-ARE) is a simple, model-based, time-aware adaptive retrieval method that helps large language models decide whether retrieval is necessary. It improves adaptive retrieval-augmented generation through in-context learning without calibration or additional training. Its instruction includes “Today is current_date()”, and it uses four demonstrations: two Yes examples for long-tail knowledge, selected with SimCSE as semantically closest long-tail questions, and two No examples of manually created questions requiring no extra information for most LLMs. This improves retrieval decisions for new world and long-tail questions, with average gains of 14.9% in retrieval accuracy and 6.7% in QA accuracy.

l: retrieval-augmented generation, RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Retrieval-augmented generation augments large language models by retrieving relevant information, and has become popular for knowledge-intensive tasks such as open-domain question-answering. It generally improves QA performance when questions require knowledge absent from LLMs, though retrieved context can be noisy or irrelevant and distract models, reducing performance. In reported experiments, GPT-4 has the highest QA accuracy despite retrieving less often than some models.

l: retrieval, RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
s: Retrieval supplies external documents or resources to augment language models when parametric knowledge is insufficient, including for questions designed to require unavailable knowledge. Rather than occurring indiscriminately as in standard RAG, it should be used only when necessary because it can add noisy or irrelevant context. Its effectiveness in RetrievalQA depends on retrieval frequency, threshold selection, and the model’s use of retrieved context before generating an answer.

l: M-RAG: Reinforcing Large Language Model Performance through Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multiple Partitions
s: The paper presents M-RAG, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework that treats database partitions as the basic units of retrieval and generation. It argues that selecting among multiple partitions can reduce retrieval noise and better emphasize crucial memories than searching an entire database. M-RAG combines a frozen large language model with multi-agent reinforcement learning: Agent-S selects a database partition, while Agent-R iteratively refines retrieved memories. Both use Deep Q-Network policies trained by evaluating generated hypotheses against references; at inference, the selected partition and refined database support generation, with complexity comparable to naive RAG aside from training-time refinement. The paper situates M-RAG alongside Naive, Advanced, and Modular RAG, reinforcement-learning work including WebGPT, InstructGPT, R3, and MMQS, and distinguishes it from Multi-source Knowledge-grounded Dialogue System by its datasets, solutions, and tasks. Experiments compare M-RAG with Naive RAG, Self-RAG, and Selfmem across summarization, machine translation, and dialogue generation, including XSum, BigPatent, JRC-Acquis, and DailyDialog. Across seven datasets and three language-model architectures, M-RAG generally produces the strongest results, reporting improvements of 11% in summarization, 8% in translation, and 12% in dialogue generation. Ablations find both agents useful; four partitions for Agent-S and three candidates for Agent-R are effective, whereas too many partitions or whole-database retrieval can hurt performance. Top-1 retrieval can match Top-3 results more quickly. The paper notes quantized models and inefficient training caused by repeated LLM queries as limitations.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, M-RAG: Reinforcing Large Language Model Performance through Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multiple Partitions
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a paradigm and framework within Large Language Models that retrieves relevant memories or information from an external database before answering questions or generating text, grounding generation in what is retrieved. It matters because whole-database retrieval can lose focus on crucial memories and introduce noise, while RAG also faces low precision, hallucination, redundancy, and context-window limitations. The work reviews Naive, Advanced, and Modular RAG, then proposes M-RAG: independent retrieval over multiple database partitions for finer-grained retrieval. M-RAG has inference complexity comparable to naive RAG, and experiments comparing Naive RAG, Self-RAG, Selfmem, and M-RAG find that adding RAG generally improves performance over no RAG. The conclusion emphasizes multiple partitions to improve retrieval and overall performance, while noting execution challenges across partitions.

l: Large Language Models, M-RAG: Reinforcing Large Language Model Performance through Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multiple Partitions
s: Large Language Models are technology used in retrieval-augmented generation: they query an external database for relevant memories, use retrieved information to guide and anchor generation, and generate summaries, responses, candidate responses, and hypotheses. They support text summarization, machine translation, and dialogue generation. In the proposed M-RAG framework, they are enhanced with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning and remain frozen during training and inference while being evaluated across three architectures, including Mixture of Experts.

The unit argues that multiple partitions can help focus retrieval on crucial memories and introduces Agent-R to generate and improve candidate memories.

l: multiple partition paradigm for RAG, M-RAG: Reinforcing Large Language Model Performance through Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multiple Partitions
s: The multiple partition paradigm for RAG organizes a database into multiple partitions, using each as the basic execution and retrieval unit instead of retrieving from the whole database. It refines retrieval by emphasizing pivotal memories to improve performance. M-RAG is introduced to support execution across partitions and address three challenges posed by this setting.

l: M-RAG, M-RAG: Reinforcing Large Language Model Performance through Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multiple Partitions
s: M-RAG is a novel multiple partition paradigm and framework for retrieval-augmented generation across multiple database partitions. It treats each partition as a retrieval entity and addresses three central challenges: database partitioning, partition selection, and memory quality. The database can be partitioned through Randomization, Clustering, Indexing, or Category; Indexing is used for summarization, Randomization for translation, and Category for dialogue generation. M-RAG then follows Retrieval-then-Generation with two agents: Agent-S selects database partitions, while Agent-R selects and refines retrieved memories. Built on multi-agent reinforcement learning, it collaboratively trains Agent-S and Agent-R end to end, aligning the training objective with text generation tasks; during inference, it supports large language model use with the refined database. Experiments use three language model architectures, 4-bit quantization, Python 3.7, and LlamaIndex, with four partitions for Agent-S and a candidate pool of three for Agent-R. Across seven datasets and three language generation tasks, text summarization, machine translation, and dialogue generation, M-RAG consistently outperforms baseline methods including Naive RAG, Self-RAG, and Selfmem. Reported improvements over the best baseline are 11% for summarization, 8% for translation, and 12% for dialogue generation, including results on XSum, JRC-Acquis, DailyDialog, and models such as Mixtral 8 × 7B, Gemma 7B, and Mistral 7B.

l: database partition, M-RAG: Reinforcing Large Language Model Performance through Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multiple Partitions
s: A database partition is a basic entity for RAG execution and retrieval in M-RAG. It supports partition selection for more specific memories, index construction and maintenance, distributed architectures, and privacy protection through access-controlled storage. M-RAG creates multiple homogeneous partitions from a single-source homogeneous dataset and studies partitioning strategies and partition numbers.

l: framework (M-RAG), M-RAG: Reinforcing Large Language Model Performance through Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multiple Partitions
s: M-RAG is a framework that leverages Large Language Models with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning to explicitly optimize different language generation tasks.

l: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning, M-RAG: Reinforcing Large Language Model Performance through Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multiple Partitions
s: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning is the basis of M-RAG, a framework with Large Language Models for explicitly optimizing language generation tasks and addressing RAG across multiple partitions. It integrates and jointly trains Agent-S and Agent-R end to end under a shared objective: producing a hypothesis similar to the reference for an input query. Agent-R refines memory, and Agent-S receives the resulting cumulative improvement. It is also noted in relation to MMQS.

l: language generation tasks, M-RAG: Reinforcing Large Language Model Performance through Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multiple Partitions
s: The language generation tasks evaluated in the experiments include text summarization, machine translation, and dialogue generation.

s: Text summarization is a language generation task evaluated as document-summary database pairs using ROUGE R-1, R-2, and R-L. It is used to assess partitioning strategies and M-RAG on XSum and BigPatent. Across experiments, M-RAG, especially with Mixtral 8×7B, achieves the strongest reported results and improves summarization performance by 11% over the best baseline.

s: Machine translation is a language generation task evaluated in motivating and broader experiments. On JRC-Acquis, it is tested with BLEU in four directions, Es→En, En→Es, De→En, and En→De, where M-RAG consistently improves results, reporting an 8% gain over the best baseline.

s: Dialogue generation is a language-generation task evaluated for database partitioning and M-RAG. In experiments on DailyDialog, it uses BLEU and Distinct metrics. M-RAG improves dialogue scores by 12% over the best baseline, while M-RAG(D), optimized with Distinct, produces more diverse dialogue.

s: models partition selection [when multiple partitions are available] Partition selection is formulated as a multi-armed bandit problem because the characteristics of each partition are only partially known at selection time. The formulation allows an agent to improve its understanding of partitions while maximizing cumulative rewards.

l: Agent-S, M-RAG: Reinforcing Large Language Model Performance through Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multiple Partitions
s: Agent-S is a partition-selection agent in M-RAG that iteratively selects one database partition for training inputs, inference queries, and retrieval. It uses reinforcement learning in a Markov Decision Process and a bandit setting to optimize its policy. Its state uses the maximum semantic similarity between an input and memories in each partition, and it shares a reward with Agent-R based on improvements in the generated hypothesis. Trained with Deep Q-Network and replay memory, it is a two-layer feedforward neural network with a 25-neuron tanh layer and an M-neuron linear layer. Experiments set M=4; removing Agent-S reduces XSum R-1. Only Agent-S and Agent-R parameters are trained, while fixed LLM queries limit training efficiency.

s: uses Markov Decision Process [to optimize the partition-selection decision policy] Reinforcement learning is used to optimize the partition-selection policy of Agent-S. The unit also uses reinforcement learning as part of the broader training process for coordinating partition selection and memory improvement.

l: Markov Decision Process, M-RAG: Reinforcing Large Language Model Performance through Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multiple Partitions
s: A framework formulating selection and refinement through states, actions, and rewards: Agent-S operates bandit-like, while Agent-R receives transition rewards as hypothesis quality changes.

l: Agent-R, M-RAG: Reinforcing Large Language Model Performance through Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multiple Partitions
s: Agent-R is a memory-refinement agent in M-RAG that improves retrieved memories after Agent-S selects a partition. It iteratively uses LLMs to generate a pool of candidate memories or responses, selects memories that improve hypothesis generation, and triggers boosting when it finds a higher-quality hypothesis. Its reward is improvement in a task-specific metric such as ROUGE or BLEU, and its cumulative reward is shared with Agent-S. Agent-R is a two-layer feedforward neural network with a 25-neuron tanh first layer and a K-neuron linear second layer; K is set to 3. It is trained with Deep Q-Network replay memory, while LLM parameters remain fixed; LLM queries limit training efficiency.
